editorial.headline: Lubricants Retail Is Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers retail sales of vehicle lubricants and cooling products—open nationally to all business scales, yet unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreign-owned business cannot register this retail activity in Bali today. That is the decisive local fact for a code that, at national level, is otherwise open to foreign investment. The activity itself is focused and practical: retail trade in lubricating oils and cooling products for motor vehicles. It belongs to the everyday maintenance economy, serving the fluids and products that keep vehicles operating within their intended temperature and lubrication requirements.

The national position is unambiguous. The activity is listed as open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. It is also open across the full range of stated business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In other words, the national framework does not reserve the activity for a particular size of enterprise, nor does it impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership in the record provided. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali changes the practical result for PMA registration. The Bali status is BLOCCATO_CLASSE_RISCHIO: blocked on risk-class grounds. At the Besar scale, every scope is classified in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium. That moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA across the province, and is described in the record as island-wide and permanent. The block is therefore not a national restriction on the retail sale of lubricants and cooling products; it is Bali’s local PMA-registration position.

For founders, the distinction deserves to be read plainly rather than softened. A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not create a route to PMA registration in Bali where the provincial moratorium applies. The activity remains nationally open across Mikro through Besar scales, but Bali’s risk-based block governs the local PMA outcome. The relevant Bali moratorium is identified as taking effect on May 13, 2026, with the stated source being the Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.
